title: The Sentry Who Slept at the Palace Gate (ZH)
summary: A young guard falls asleep on duty after nursing his sick mother all night. Birbal saves the soldier from the executioner's sword.
full_text:
During an unannounced midnight inspection of the Agra palace ramparts, Emperor Akbar discovered a nineteen-year-old sentry named Dilip slumped against the stone parapet, sound asleep with his spear lying in the dust.

Akbar's military code was absolute and unforgiving: any sentry caught sleeping on watch was guilty of treason and sentenced to be beheaded at dawn.

The next morning, Dilip was brought before the court in chains. The young soldier wept, but did not deny his fault.

Akbar raised his hand to pronounce the death sentence: 'By the laws of our army, you must die.'

Birbal stepped forward: 'Sire, the law is just, but justice must examine the heart before it swings the sword. Dilip has served in the royal guard for three years without a single blemish. Why did he sleep last night?'

Birbal questioned the soldier's commander and neighbors.

The commander revealed: 'Sire, Dilip's widowed mother was stricken with cholera three nights ago. For seventy-two hours, the boy stayed awake by her bedside, bathing her feverish brow, carrying medicine, and weeping over her. He reported for duty last night without having slept for three days, refusing to take sick leave because he needed his daily wage to buy her milk.'

The entire court fell silent.

Birbal turned to Akbar with tears in his eyes:

'Sire, Dilip did not sleep out of treason or drunkenness. His body collapsed under the sacred weight of filial devotion and desperate poverty.

'A boy who loves his mother so deeply will fight to the death to protect the Emperor who shows his mother mercy! If we execute our most devoted sons for human exhaustion, we murder the very soul of our people!'

Akbar's stern face softened. He wiped a tear from his eye, descended from the throne, and lifted the young soldier to his feet:

'Dilip, your devotion to your mother honors this empire.'

Akbar pardoned the soldier, granted his mother a monthly medical allowance, and thanked Birbal for proving that royal mercy is the true strength of an army.
